newsitem.title: INDIA: India vows Kashmir killers will face consequences.
newsitem.headline: India vows Kashmir killers will face consequences.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Monday condemned the killings of seven Hindus in the troubled Himalayan region of Kashmir, vowing that the attackers would not "escape the consequences".

"I wish to emphasise that the perpetrators of this act of terror shall not escape the consequences of their horrible crime," Deve Gowda said in a statement issued before he left for a three-day visit to Russia.

"Their masters abroad, who aid and abet cross-border terrorism, should understand that the entire Indian nation stands together in the defence of the territorial integrity and secular unity of the country," Deve Gowda said. The Indian leader's statement was timed four days before Indian and Pakistani diplomats sit down to resume talks broken off three years ago that are likely to include the acrimonious subject of Kashmir.

The killings late on Friday of seven Hindus in Kashmir marked a fresh outbreak of violence. One Indian soldier and four separatist guerrillas died in a 12-hour gun battle on the outskirts of Kashmir's summer capital Srinagar, police said on Sunday.
Violence against Hindus in the province, the only Moslem-majority state in mainly Hindu India, is usually blamed on Islamic separatists.

Pakistan has fought two wars with India over the region since the two nations became independent from British rule in 1947. It denies Indian charges that it arms and trains Kashmiri separatist guerrillas.

The attack at Sangrampur, a village in Budgam district 20 km (13 miles) southwest of Srinagar, was the first major act of violence against Hindus since September last year when India held the first provincial elections in the state since 1987.

Deve Gowda referred to the elections in his statement, saying: "The full restoration of democratic government in Jammu and Kashmir has opened a new chapter and has decisively defeated the designs of the terrorists and their masters abroad."

Police said in the Friday attack, 15 unidentified gunmen encircled Hindu homes in Sangrampur village and forced eight males out, saying security officials wanted to talk to them. The men were shot down just outside the village. One survived.
No separatist group has claimed responsibility for the killings, described by police as the biggest such incident involving local Hindus.
More than a dozen militant groups are fighting New Delhi's rule in Jammu and Kashmir state, mainly India's only Moslem majority province.
Kashmir's leading separatist organisation, the All-Parties' Hurriyat (freedom) Conference, which brings together some 30 religious and political groups, has condemned the incident.
"The killing is the handiwork of anti-movement activists who want to defame the ongoing freedom struggle of Kashmir," a Hurriyat spokesman said on Saturday.

More than 300,000 minority Hindus, called Pandits in the Himalayan valley, fled Kashmir after the beginning of the rebellion in 1990 in the region, where violence linked to insurgency has claimed more than 20,000 lives.
